description: A single die rolls on screen, then multiplies to dozens, then hundreds. Results scatter onto a number line, then lift into 2D, 3D, and finally a swirling high-dimensional point cloud. The cloud pulses with hidden structure.

steps.label: single-die
steps.description: A single die tumbles across the screen, lands on a face, value appears on a number line
steps.narration_spoken: One die. Six faces. You already know the odds.

steps.label: many-dice
steps.description: Dozens of dice roll simultaneously, results scatter as dots on a number line forming an uneven histogram
steps.narration_spoken: But throw a hundred dice at once. The results cluster into a shape... a pattern hiding inside randomness.

steps.label: higher-dimensions
steps.description: Number line lifts into 2D scatter, then 3D rotating point cloud. Points form a structured blob with density variations.
steps.narration_spoken: Push this further. Thousands of random numbers, arranged across hundreds of dimensions. The cloud has geometry. Can you

steps.label: question-posed
steps.description: Cloud pulses. Text overlay fades in: 'What language describes this?'
steps.narration_spoken: What mathematical language captures the shape of randomness? That is our question today.

steps.label: connection-tease
steps.description: Quick flash: a generative model pulls a point from the cloud, and an image materializes beside it
steps.narration_spoken: Aswin, every generative model you want to understand starts right here... inside this cloud.

description: A clean image dissolves into noise through forward diffusion steps. Then the process reverses — noise sharpens back into the image. Camera zooms into the noise, revealing each pixel is a sample from a bell curve. Lesson roadmap appears.

steps.label: diffusion-forward
steps.description: A clean photograph dissolves through five noise steps into pure static grain
steps.narration_spoken: A diffusion model adds noise until an image becomes static. Pure chaos.

steps.label: diffusion-reverse
steps.description: The noise reverses through five denoising steps back to a coherent image
steps.narration_spoken: Then it reverses the process. Step by step, structure returns from noise.

steps.label: zoom-into-noise
steps.description: Camera zooms into the noise layer. Individual pixels enlarge, each connected by an arrow to a point on a bell curve
steps.narration_spoken: But where does the starting noise come from? Each pixel is a random draw from a Gaussian distribution.

steps.label: bridge-to-lesson
steps.description: Bell curve highlighted with labels. Text appears: 'Random Variables + PDF'
steps.narration_spoken: To control that draw, you need two tools. Random variables and probability density functions.

steps.label: roadmap
steps.description: Lesson roadmap fades in: four connected nodes labeled RV → PMF → PDF → Gaussian
steps.narration_spoken: Those are exactly what we build today. The foundation beneath every generative model.

description: Left side shows a bubble labeled 'Experiment' containing icons (coin, die, thermometer). Right side shows a number line labeled 'Real Numbers'. Arrows map specific outcomes to numbers. The function is labeled X. A highlight emphasizes that randomness lives in the experiment, not the function.

steps.label: experiment-space
steps.description: Bubble on left labeled 'Experiment' fills with icons: a coin, a die, a thermometer
steps.narration_spoken: Start with an experiment. A coin flip, a die roll, measuring temperature... anything with uncertain outcomes.

steps.label: number-line
steps.description: Number line appears on the right side, labeled 'Real Numbers' with tick marks
steps.narration_spoken: On the other side, a number line. Every possible numerical value lives here.

steps.label: mapping-arrows
steps.description: Animated arrows draw from 'Heads' to 1, 'Tails' to 0. Die faces map to 1 through 6.
steps.narration_spoken: A random variable is a function. It takes each outcome and assigns it a number. Heads becomes one, tails becomes zero.

steps.label: formal-label
steps.description: The function is labeled with a large capital X. Formula appears: X maps from omega to the reals.
steps.narration_spoken: We write it as capital X. A function from the set of all outcomes to the real number line. Why capital? Because the valu

steps.label: key-insight
steps.description: Highlight pulse on the experiment side: 'Randomness is HERE'. The arrow and number line dim to secondary. Text: 'The fun
steps.narration_spoken: Here is the crucial point. The function itself is deterministic. The randomness lives in which outcome nature selects. T

description: Die rolling animation with mapping to number line. Coin flips with 0/1 mapping. A counter showing 'emails received today' mapping to {0,1,2,3,...}. All three have dots on the number line with visible gaps between values.

steps.label: die-experiment
steps.description: Die rolls, lands on 4. Arrow animates from the face to the number 4 on a number line.
steps.narration_spoken: Roll a standard die. The random variable X maps the top face to its number. This roll gave us four.

steps.label: all-outcomes
steps.description: All six die faces appear, each with an arrow pointing to its dot on {1,2,3,4,5,6}. Gaps between dots are highlighted.
steps.narration_spoken: Six faces mean six possible values. One through six, nothing in between. What sits between three and four? Nothing. Empt

steps.label: discrete-definition
steps.description: Dots glow on the number line at exactly {1,2,3,4,5,6}. Label appears: 'Discrete Random Variable'.
steps.narration_spoken: When a random variable lands only on isolated dots... we call it discrete. Countable, separated values with gaps between

steps.label: coin-example
steps.description: Coin flips. Heads maps to 1, Tails maps to 0. Two dots on the number line.
steps.narration_spoken: A coin flip is even simpler. Two outcomes, two dots. Zero or one, nothing else.

steps.label: counting-example
steps.description: Email counter increments: 0, 1, 2, 3, ... Dots extend rightward on the number line with gaps.
steps.narration_spoken: Counting emails received today? Zero, one, two, three... The dots go on forever, but each is isolated. Still discrete.

description: Four scenario cards appear: (A) Number of heads in 10 flips, (B) Exact height of a person, (C) Typos on a page, (D) Waiting time for next bus. Cards flip to reveal discrete (dots) or continuous (filled interval) classifications.

steps.label: show-scenarios
steps.description: Four cards slide in from the sides, face down with letters A through D
steps.narration_spoken: Time to test your intuition, Aswin. Four experiments, four random variables.

steps.label: reveal-cards
steps.description: Cards flip to reveal: A) Heads in 10 flips, B) Exact height, C) Typos on a page, D) Bus wait time
steps.narration_spoken: Number of heads in ten flips. Exact height of a stranger. Typo count on a page. Waiting time for the next bus.

steps.label: pose-question
steps.description: Question text overlays: 'Which are discrete? Which are continuous?' Cards pulse waiting for selection.
steps.narration_spoken: Which ones land on isolated dots? Which could take any value in a range?

steps.label: student-thinks
steps.description: Pause state. A subtle hint fades in: 'Can the value fall between two neighbors?'
steps.narration_spoken: Think carefully. The key question is... can the value fall between two neighboring possibilities?

steps.label: reveal-answer
steps.description: A and C glow blue with dot patterns beneath. B and D glow orange with filled interval lines beneath.
steps.narration_spoken: Heads and typos are counts... discrete. Height and waiting time can be any value in an interval... continuous. The gaps

description: A die rolls repeatedly. After each roll, a histogram bar increments. The simulation accelerates: 10 rolls produce a jagged histogram, 100 rolls smooth it, 1000 rolls converge to near-equal bars at 1/6 each. Bars are labeled with fractions. A 'Total = 1' counter glows at the top.

steps.label: ten-rolls
steps.description: Die rolls 10 times in quick succession. A histogram with 6 bins forms, bars are uneven and jagged.
steps.narration_spoken: Roll a fair die ten times. The histogram is messy. Some numbers appeared twice, others not at all.

steps.label: hundred-rolls
steps.description: Roll counter accelerates to 100. Bars grow more evenly, approaching similar heights.
steps.narration_spoken: A hundred rolls. Can you see the shape forming? The bars start evening out.

steps.label: thousand-rolls
steps.description: Counter hits 1000. All six bars converge to nearly equal heights, each close to 1/6.
steps.narration_spoken: A thousand rolls... and every bar hovers near one-sixth. The true probabilities emerge from the chaos.

steps.label: pmf-label
steps.description: Bars labeled with exact fractions. Title text fades in: 'PMF of a Fair Die'.
steps.narration_spoken: This histogram has a name. The probability mass function. It assigns a probability to each possible value.

steps.label: mass-metaphor
steps.description: Each bar glows with the word 'mass' inside. A counter at the top accumulates: 1/6 + 1/6 + ... = 1.0.
steps.narration_spoken: Think of probability as mass. Each bar holds some. The total across all bars... exactly one.

description: Mathematical definition of PMF built piece by piece. P(X=x) notation appears large. Two properties animate in: non-negativity and sum-to-one. Then a two-dice PMF histogram appears with a triangular shape, peak at 7 highlighted. An arrow connects to a neural network icon representing token prediction

steps.label: definition
steps.description: Large text: P(X = x). Beneath it: 'The probability that random variable X takes the value x.'
steps.narration_spoken: Capital P, X equals small x. This is the PMF. It answers one question... what is the probability X lands exactly on this

steps.label: property-nonneg
steps.description: First property animates in: P(X=x) is greater than or equal to zero for all x. A bar chart shows no bars below the axis.
steps.narration_spoken: First property. Every probability is zero or positive. Negative probability would make no physical sense.

steps.label: property-sum
steps.description: Second property: sum over all x of P(X=x) equals 1. An animated accumulator adds bar heights, reaching 1.0.
steps.narration_spoken: Second property. Add up every bar in the histogram. The total must equal one. All the probability mass is accounted for.

steps.label: two-dice-pmf
steps.description: Two-dice PMF histogram appears: triangular shape from sum 2 to 12. Bar at 7 glows brightest. Labels: 6 ways to make 7, 1
steps.narration_spoken: Two dice summed. The PMF is no longer flat. Seven has the most mass... six ways to make seven. Two and twelve? Only one

steps.label: ml-connection
steps.description: Arrow from PMF to a neural network icon. Text: 'Token prediction = PMF over vocabulary.'
steps.narration_spoken: Why care? Every discrete distribution in machine learning is a PMF. Token prediction in a language model? That is a PMF

description: The two-dice PMF histogram extrudes into 3D columns, forming a probability landscape. Camera rotates to show peaks and valleys. A second landscape (loaded die) appears for comparison. Both landscapes shown side by side with the label 'Shape = Distribution'.

steps.label: flat-histogram
steps.description: Standard 2D PMF histogram of two dice sums. Bars of varying heights.
steps.narration_spoken: The two-dice PMF from before. Bars of different heights across possible sums.

steps.label: extrude-3d
steps.description: Bars extrude into 3D columns. Camera rotates 45 degrees to reveal the probability landscape as terrain.
steps.narration_spoken: Lift these bars into three dimensions. A landscape of probability. Mountains where outcomes are likely, valleys where th

steps.label: navigate-terrain
steps.description: Camera flies over the terrain. The peak at sum 7 glows. A flag plants on the summit.
steps.narration_spoken: The peak at seven... that is where the probability mass concentrates. If you had to bet, where would you place your chip

steps.label: loaded-landscape
steps.description: A second 3D landscape appears: loaded die PMF. One face dominates with a tall spike, others are low.
steps.narration_spoken: A loaded die produces a different landscape. One face dominates. The terrain is lopsided, asymmetric.

steps.label: shape-is-distribution
steps.description: Both landscapes side by side. Text appears: 'Shape = Distribution'.
steps.narration_spoken: The shape of the landscape is the distribution. Reading these shapes... that is the core skill we are building.

description: A complete PMF table for the sum of two fair dice (values 2-12 with exact probabilities). The question P(X >= 10) is highlighted. Bars for 10, 11, 12 glow while others dim. After the student answers, the three bars merge into a single highlighted region labeled 1/6.

steps.label: show-table
steps.description: Full PMF table fades in: two columns, sum values 2 through 12 with probabilities as fractions of 36.
steps.narration_spoken: The complete PMF for the sum of two fair dice. Every sum from two to twelve, with its exact probability.

steps.label: pose-problem
steps.description: Question text highlights in bold: 'What is P(X >= 10)?'
steps.narration_spoken: Your task, Aswin. What is the probability the sum is ten or greater?

steps.label: hint-visual
steps.description: Bars for 10, 11, and 12 glow bright. All other bars dim to 20% opacity.
steps.narration_spoken: Which bars do you need? Isolate them. Sum their heights.

steps.label: student-calculates
steps.description: Pause state. Hint text appears: '3/36 + 2/36 + 1/36 = ?'
steps.narration_spoken: P of ten is three out of thirty-six. P of eleven is two out of thirty-six. P of twelve... one out of thirty-six.

steps.label: reveal-answer
steps.description: The three bars merge into a single highlighted region. Answer appears: 6/36 = 1/6.
steps.narration_spoken: Add them up. Six out of thirty-six, which simplifies to one-sixth. The PMF made that calculation mechanical.

description: Animated transition from discrete to continuous. A 6-sided die PMF has wide bars. Switch to 20-sided: thinner bars. 100-sided: slivers tracing a curve. Infinite: bars dissolve into a smooth continuous curve. A single point is highlighted with P = 0.

steps.label: six-bars
steps.description: Fair die PMF: six wide, equal-height bars on a number line from 1 to 6.
steps.narration_spoken: Start familiar. Six outcomes, six bars. Each bar has real height, real width.

steps.label: twenty-bars
steps.description: Bars morph: twenty thinner bars appear for a 20-sided die. Still visible individual bars.
steps.narration_spoken: A twenty-sided die. More outcomes, thinner bars. Each bar shrinks, but they still sum to one.

steps.label: hundred-bars
steps.description: One hundred very thin bars. The tops trace out a nearly smooth curve.
steps.narration_spoken: A hundred sides. The bars are slivers now. Squint... and the tops trace out a curve.

steps.label: infinite-limit
steps.description: Bars dissolve entirely. A smooth continuous curve remains. Label: 'From bars to curve'.
steps.narration_spoken: Push to infinity. The bars vanish. A smooth curve remains. This is the leap from discrete to continuous.

steps.label: zero-probability
steps.description: Arrow points to a single point on the curve. An infinitely thin line has zero area. Label: 'P(X = exactly this) = 0'.
steps.narration_spoken: And here is the strange consequence. Any single exact value has probability zero. The bar has no width to hold mass.

description: Three examples of continuous random variables with smooth distribution curves: temperature (bell curve), human height (bell curve), pixel intensity in [0,1] (arbitrary curve). A number line comparison shows dots (discrete) versus filled solid interval (continuous).

steps.label: temperature
steps.description: Thermometer icon with a smooth bell curve beside it. Labels: 22.1, 22.13, 22.137 degrees.
steps.narration_spoken: Temperature at noon tomorrow. It could be 22.1 degrees, or 22.13, or 22.137. Infinite precision, infinite possibilities.

steps.label: height
steps.description: Height chart with measuring tape and smooth distribution curve.
steps.narration_spoken: Human height. Not just 170 centimeters... but 170.34 or 170.342. The number line is fully filled.

steps.label: pixel-intensity
steps.description: Single pixel square with a [0,1] range slider and a distribution curve above it. Arrow to a generative model icon.
steps.narration_spoken: A pixel value in a generated image. Any real number between zero and one. This is the continuous random variable generat

steps.label: no-gaps
steps.description: Split comparison: top row shows discrete dots with gaps, bottom row shows solid filled interval. Gap arrows highlight th
steps.narration_spoken: Where discrete variables leave gaps... continuous variables fill every point. What happened to the spaces between dots?

steps.label: definition
steps.description: Formal text appears: 'X is continuous if it can take any value in an interval.'
steps.narration_spoken: Continuous means the random variable can land anywhere within an interval. No gaps, no jumps.

description: A smooth bell curve with y-axis initially unlabeled. 'Probability?' label appears near the peak, gets crossed out, replaced by 'Density'. steps.label: the-curve
steps.description: Smooth bell curve on screen. Y-axis has no label. Question mark floats near the peak.
steps.narration_spoken: This smooth curve replaced our histogram. But what does the height actually mean?

steps.label: not-probability
steps.description: Label 'Probability?' fades in near the peak, then a red X crosses it out. 'Density' replaces it in green.
steps.narration_spoken: The height is not probability. Repeat that. The height of the PDF at a point is not the probability of that point. It is

steps.label: density-analogy
steps.description: A horizontal metal rod appears below the curve. Thick sections align with high-density regions. Thin sections align with
steps.narration_spoken: Think of a metal rod with varying thickness. Dense regions are heavier per centimeter. Similarly, dense regions of the P

steps.label: can-exceed-one
steps.description: A narrow, tall spike PDF appears. The peak clearly exceeds height 1.0. A horizontal line at y=1 shows the peak above it.
steps.narration_spoken: Density can exceed one. Surprising? A thin interval packed with probability has high density. The constraint is on area,

steps.label: area-preview
steps.description: Return to bell curve. A region between two bounds is shaded blue. Area label shows 0.3.
steps.narration_spoken: The probability lives in the area. Shade a region under the curve... that area equals the probability of landing in that

description: PDF formal definition built piece by piece. f(x) notation appears. Two properties: non-negativity and total integral = 1. The probability formula P(a <= X <= b) = integral of f(x) from a to b, with a shaded region animation. Side-by-side comparison: PMF sum vs PDF integral.

steps.label: pdf-symbol
steps.description: Large text: f(x). Label below: 'Probability Density Function'. Contrast with P(X=x) from PMF, shown dimmed.
steps.narration_spoken: We write the PDF as lowercase f of x. Small f, not capital P. Capital P gives probability. Small f gives density.

steps.label: property-nonneg
steps.description: First rule appears: f(x) >= 0 for all x. The curve never dips below the x-axis.
steps.narration_spoken: First rule. The density is never negative. The curve never dips below the x-axis.

steps.label: property-integral
steps.description: Second rule: integral from negative infinity to positive infinity of f(x) dx = 1. Full area under curve shades to show t
steps.narration_spoken: Second rule. The total area under the entire curve equals one. Compare this to the PMF... same idea, integral replaces s

steps.label: probability-formula
steps.description: P(a <= X <= b) = integral from a to b of f(x) dx. Region between a and b shades on the curve.
steps.narration_spoken: To get actual probability... integrate. P of X between a and b is the area under f from a to b.

steps.label: pmf-vs-pdf-parallel
steps.description: Split view: left shows PMF with summation symbol, right shows PDF with integral symbol. Both arrows point to 'Probabilit
steps.narration_spoken: PMF sums bars. PDF integrates area. Same logic, different mechanics. Discrete sums become continuous integrals.

description: Standard normal bell curve. Progressive shading: left tail (small area ~16%), center region -1 to 1 (large area ~68%), a single point at x=0 (zero area), then a sliding fixed-width window that moves across the curve showing varying area size.

steps.label: full-curve
steps.description: Standard normal bell curve. No shading. Clean axes.
steps.narration_spoken: A bell-shaped PDF. The most famous curve in all of probability.

steps.label: shade-left-tail
steps.description: Region X < -1 shades in blue. Area label: approximately 16%.
steps.narration_spoken: Shade everything below negative one. That small area... about sixteen percent. The probability of landing in the left ta

steps.label: shade-center
steps.description: Clear previous shade. Region -1 to 1 shades in green. Area label: approximately 68%.
steps.narration_spoken: Shade between negative one and positive one. That wide region holds sixty-eight percent of all the probability.

steps.label: shade-single-point
steps.description: Clear previous shade. An infinitely thin vertical line at x=0. Area label: 0%.
steps.narration_spoken: Shade a single point. X equals exactly zero. The line has no width... so the area is zero. Why we need intervals.

steps.label: sliding-window
steps.description: A fixed-width rectangle slides left to right across the curve. Area value updates in real time — large near the peak, sm
steps.narration_spoken: Slide a fixed-width window across the curve. Near the peak, the area is large. In the tails, the area shrinks. Where wou

description: Side-by-side comparison: discrete PMF with P(X=3) = 1/6 bar highlighted (positive width), and continuous PDF with infinitely thin line at X=3.0 (zero width). The question asks why exact-value probability is zero. A hint shows width shrinking to zero. The reveal animation shows width → 0 × height = 0

steps.label: recall-discrete
steps.description: Discrete PMF on left. Bar at X=3 highlighted with label P(X=3) = 1/6. The bar has visible width.
steps.narration_spoken: For a fair die, P of X equals three is one-sixth. A real, positive number. The bar has height and width.

steps.label: contrast-continuous
steps.description: Continuous PDF on right. An infinitely thin vertical line at X=3.0. No visible width.
steps.narration_spoken: For a continuous variable, P of X equals exactly three-point-zero... is zero. The line has no width.

steps.label: pose-question
steps.description: Question text: 'Why must P(X = exact value) = 0 for a continuous RV?' Think bubble appears.
steps.narration_spoken: Aswin, explain why. Why must the probability of any single exact value be zero?

steps.label: student-thinks
steps.description: Pause for thinking. Hint fades in: 'Think about area...'
steps.narration_spoken: Hint... probability is area. What is the area of a region with zero width?

steps.label: explanation
steps.description: Animation: bar width shrinks from 0.5 to 0.1 to 0.01 to 0, area counter drops to zero. Text: 'Zero width times finite he
steps.narration_spoken: Zero width times any finite height gives zero area. No area means no probability. This is not a flaw... it is the nature

steps.label: setup-pdf
steps.description: Triangle-shaped curve: straight line from (0,0) to (1,2). Label: f(x) = 2x for 0 <= x <= 1.
steps.narration_spoken: A simple PDF. f of x equals two x, for x between zero and one. A straight line, rising from zero to two.

steps.label: verify-valid
steps.description: Triangle shaded. Calculation: area = one-half times base times height = one-half times 1 times 2 = 1. Check mark.
steps.narration_spoken: First, verify it is a valid PDF. The area is a triangle. Base one, height two. One-half times one times two... equals on

steps.label: ask-probability
steps.description: Question appears: P(0.5 <= X <= 1). The region from 0.5 to 1 shades under the triangle.
steps.narration_spoken: What is the probability X falls between one-half and one? Shade that region. We need its area.

steps.label: integrate
steps.description: Step-by-step integration: integral from 0.5 to 1 of 2x dx. Antiderivative: x squared. Evaluate: 1 squared minus 0.5 squa
steps.narration_spoken: Integrate two x from one-half to one. The antiderivative is x squared. One squared minus one-half squared equals... thre

steps.label: interpret
steps.description: Shaded region labeled 0.75. Remaining small triangle labeled 0.25. Arrow to generative model icon.

steps.narration_spoken: Two worlds of randomness. Left, discrete. Right, continuous. Same goals, different tools.

steps.label: variable-type
steps.description: Left: isolated dots on number line. Right: solid filled interval on number line.
steps.narration_spoken: Discrete lands on dots. Continuous fills intervals. The random variable itself dictates which world you enter.

steps.description: Left: PMF bar chart. Right: PDF smooth curve. Labels highlight: 'heights = probabilities' vs 'heights = densities'.

description: The Gaussian bell curve rises from the x-axis. Its formula appears with mu and sigma labeled. The curve slides left and right as mu changes. steps.label: bell-appears

steps.narration_spoken: The Gaussian. The bell curve. The single most important PDF in all of machine learning.

steps.narration_spoken: Its formula has two parameters. Mu shifts the center left or right. Sigma controls the width... the spread of the bell.

steps.narration_spoken: Change mu. The entire bell slides along the number line. The shape stays the same. Only the center moves.

steps.label: change-sigma

steps.description: Standard Gaussian with mu=0, sigma=1 labeled clearly. Clean axes with sigma markers at -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3.

steps.narration_spoken: The empirical rule. Sixty-eight percent within one sigma. Ninety-five within two. Ninety-nine point seven within three.
